question: Can every major Transformer parameter group be interpreted without inputs by expressing its action in the model's vocabulary embedding space?

key_findings.claim: The framework rewrites feed-forward keys and values plus attention query-key and value-output interactions as vocabulary-space objects.
key_findings.evidence: Inserting an embedding right inverse around hidden-space products yields projected vectors or token-by-token transition matrices; Table 1 gives exact and transpose-based approximations for every component and subhead.

key_findings.claim: The practical interpretation uses the embedding transpose, not the algebraically exact pseudoinverse.
key_findings.evidence: Because explanations retain only top-k vocabulary logits, the pseudoinverse reconstructs dense vectors but performs poorly after truncation. The transpose is empirically a better keep-k robust inverse for GPT-2-like embeddings.

key_findings.claim: Static projections recover recognizable lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns in GPT-2 parameters.
key_findings.evidence: Manual top-token and top-token-pair inspections identify heads associated with morphology, geography, gender, orthography, parts of speech, and topics; selected feed-forward key-value pairs share topical vocabulary.

key_findings.claim: Activated static parameter vectors overlap a hidden state's vocabulary projection more than randomly paired hidden states.
key_findings.evidence: On 60 IMDB examples with GPT-2 medium, the R-k statistic compares top-k vocabulary overlap for the most active keys, values, and attention subheads; aligned layer/token states exceed random-state controls across layers.

key_findings.claim: Embedding-space comparison aligns corresponding layers of independently pretrained BERT instances.
key_findings.evidence: Projected parameter correlations across MultiBERT seeds, followed by Hungarian matching, generally pair the same layer indices across all parameter groups; direct feature-space matching appears unstructured.

key_findings.claim: Zero-shot model stitching is possible but unreliable.
key_findings.evidence: A fixed embedding-space map transfers hidden states from 24-layer GPT-2 medium into the top three IMDB-fine-tuned layers of 12-layer GPT-2 base. Only 3 of 11 random trials significantly exceed chance, reaching about 70% accuracy.

key_findings.claim: Vocabulary projection is a suggestive label generator, not a causal explanation of computation.
key_findings.evidence: The analysis ignores biases and LayerNorm, assumes a linear language-model head and tied or comparable embeddings, and validates many claims through selected top-k words. It does not intervene on projected features to show they mediate model behavior.

method.core_idea: Use the vocabulary embedding matrix as a common coordinate system for static Transformer parameters and cross-model representations.
method.mechanism: Hidden states are mapped to vocabulary logits with E and reconstructed with a right inverse. Inserting E E-prime identities turns feed-forward vectors and attention bilinear/transition matrices into token vectors or token-pair matrices. For readable top-k explanations, E-transpose approximates the inverse; projected correlations support layer alignment, and E_A E_B-plus supports stitching.
assumptions: The embedding matrix has adequate rank and its vocabulary directions form a meaningful explanatory basis.
Top-k vocabulary logits preserve the semantics of a dense projected vector.
Ignoring bias and normalization does not qualitatively change parameter action.
Models compared share a tokenizer and sufficiently compatible embedding semantics.

techniques.role: Re-expresses hidden-space operations as vocabulary-space interactions.
Combines query-key and value-output weights into interpretable bilinear or transition maps.
Chooses a transpose approximation optimized for truncated vocabulary explanations.
Matches layers across model seeds using embedding-space correlations.
Transfers representations between differently sized models without fitting an alignment map.

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 base, medium, and large parameter inspection.
evaluations.metric: Human coherence and overlap of top-k projected vocabulary items or pairs.
evaluations.result: Numerous attention and feed-forward components admit recognizable token-level descriptions.
evaluations.baseline: Unprojected hidden-space weights, which have no vocabulary interpretation.

evaluations.metric: R-k overlap between activated parameter projections and aligned versus random hidden-state projections.
evaluations.result: Aligned states show higher vocabulary overlap for all tested parameter groups across most layers.

evaluations.setting: Pairs of 12-layer MultiBERT models trained from different random seeds.
evaluations.metric: Hungarian layer matching from mean absolute parameter-projection correlations.
evaluations.result: Corresponding layer indices align in embedding space across parameter groups, unlike raw feature-space comparisons.

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 medium stitched to three IMDB-fine-tuned GPT-2 base layers.
evaluations.metric: Binary sentiment accuracy over stitch depth and 11 random runs.
evaluations.result: Three runs reach roughly 70% without alignment training; most remain near the 50% baseline.

limitations: Most evidence concerns small GPT-2 and BERT-era models, not modern gated, untied, multilingual, or multimodal architectures.
The framework omits bias and LayerNorm and is theoretically cleanest for a linear tied language-model head.
Top-k token inspection is subjective and vulnerable to cherry-picking, stereotypes, and correlated vocabulary artifacts.
Projection cannot resolve polysemantic superpositions into independent causal features.
The stitching result succeeds in only a minority of trials and uses one binary classification task.
Sharing a tokenizer does not guarantee that two models assign the same geometry or meaning to token directions.
failure_modes: Untied or nonlinear output heads invalidate the assumed canonical vocabulary coordinates.
Anisotropic embeddings can make generic high-frequency tokens dominate projections.
A parameter can have an interpretable projection yet participate in a different computation under context and normalization.
Top-k truncation can discard distributed evidence and reverse apparent similarity.
Cross-model stitching can land off the receiving model's activation manifold.
Human-readable token labels can conceal causal irrelevance.
reusable_insights: Distinguish algebraic reconstruction quality from explanation quality after top-k truncation.
Validate static interpretations against activations and causal interventions, not only readable token lists.
A shared output basis can provide a cheap first-pass alignment across related models.
Report unsuccessful stitching seeds and sensitivity, since selective successes substantially overstate reliability.
Audit projected token sets for embedding frequency and social-bias artifacts.
open_questions: How well does the method scale to current untied, gated, normalized, and multilingual LLMs?
Can causal ablation validate that projected vocabulary features mediate predictions?
Can learned sparse dictionaries replace vocabulary directions while retaining cross-model comparability?
What predicts whether zero-shot stitching will work before evaluation?
How should uncertainty in a top-k parameter explanation be calibrated?

competitive_landscape.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest precursor using the output vocabulary to interpret feed-forward updates.
competitive_landscape.difference: Geva et al. analyze how MLP values affect predictions during forward passes; Dar et al. generalize static projection to keys, all attention weights, model alignment, and stitching.

competitive_landscape.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing vocabulary-lens method correcting layerwise representation drift.
competitive_landscape.difference: The tuned lens learns affine translators from intermediate activations to logits and is input-dependent; this work projects parameters with a fixed embedding map and requires no fitting for interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current alternative basis for decomposing polysemantic internal representations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sparse autoencoders learn a feature dictionary from activations and can separate superposed concepts; embedding-space analysis uses fixed vocabulary directions and can inspect weights without an input corpus.

competitive_landscape.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later attention-focused interpretability study with causal circuit validation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kissane et al. decompose attention outputs across several models and test discovered variables in a known circuit; Dar et al. directly label attention parameter matrices but provide no comparable causal validation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a unified zero-pass vocabulary-space interpretation of all Transformer parameter groups, plus input-independent cross-model alignment and stitching.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The algebraic unification and cross-model applications are genuinely inventive and cheap. The semantic conclusions remain provisional because vocabulary projections conflate explanation with basis similarity and lack causal tests; sparse learned features and tuned lenses now provide stronger alternatives for several use cases.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 45-page extraction, including derivation, keep-k inverse analysis, all interpretation and alignment experiments, stitching, limitations, and qualitative appendices. Primary arXiv sources on feed-forward vocabulary updates, the tuned lens, and sparse-autoencoder interpretation were checked on 2026-08-23.
